TIPA: A ladder of inflation-protected Treasury bonds with maturities running up to 2030, designed to pay out income as the rungs come due. It is a spend-down style holding for money earmarked for around 2030, with inflation protection built into every bond.
HIAI: A concentrated portfolio of US stocks chosen by artificial intelligence models hunting for high-conviction ideas across technology, retail, health care and more. The AI-driven picks mean the lineup can look unusual and change as the models change their minds.
GDOC: Health care companies working on the field's future: gene-based medicine, precision treatments, robotic procedures and digital health, from giants to small innovators. It is a growth bet on medical innovation, so breakthroughs and trial failures can move it sharply.
TBX: A daily bet against intermediate Treasury bonds, designed to rise when seven to ten year Treasury prices fall and interest rates climb. It resets daily and is meant for short-term trades or hedging, not for holding through calm markets.
FMQQ: Internet and e-commerce companies in emerging and frontier markets, from online marketplaces and food delivery to digital payments, led by consumer and finance names. It reaches younger, faster-growing online economies that the big emerging market funds often underweight.
XMAY: Options on the S&P 500 set to enhance gains up to a cap while moderating losses over a one-year period ending each May. It softens the ride for cautious investors, trading away part of strong rallies for a cushion against moderate drops.
PJFM: Mid-sized US companies picked through a mix of fundamental research and systematic portfolio building, spread across technology, finance, industry and health care. It is a focused mid-cap portfolio, so the managers' stock choices matter more than the mid-cap market itself.
TNXT: Companies leading in innovation across developed markets, from chip and software giants to medical pioneers, with technology near half the fund and health care about a quarter. It is a growth portfolio built around new technology and business models, so it swings more than the broad market.
BUFX: A ladder of twelve monthly buffer funds on the S&P 500, each aiming for roughly double the index's gains up to a cap with a buffer against the first 15 percent of losses. Staggering the start dates smooths the timing risk of buying protection all at once.
RMCA: California municipal bonds from schools, housing agencies, airports and hospitals across the state, paying interest exempt from both federal and California income tax. It is aimed at California taxpayers, and the single-state focus means state finances matter more than in a national fund.
FFDI: Growth companies in developed markets outside the US, chosen with Fidelity's fundamental research, with banks and industrial firms the biggest slices. It aims to beat plain international funds through stock picking, across Europe, Japan and other developed economies.
RSMV: US growth companies chosen for relative strength, meaning their prices have been outrunning peers, with volatility management that can trim risk when markets get rough. The approach leans into winners, so it can be caught out when market leadership suddenly flips.
LCIV: Large foreign companies bought through US-listed depositary receipts, screened for value, with financials, energy, health care and consumer brands all represented. Using receipts avoids foreign exchanges and currencies directly, though the stocks still move with their home markets.
MFSX: Short-term municipal bonds from US states and cities, paying interest exempt from federal income tax. The short maturities keep price swings small when interest rates move, making it a tax-aware parking spot for cautious money.
MCHS: Chinese companies picked as innovators in their products, technology or business models, mostly in industry and technology, from chip equipment to factory automation. It is a focused growth bet on China's inventive side, with the usual political and market risks of the region.
MBSX: Fixed-rate mortgage bonds backed by US home loans and guaranteed by government-sponsored housing agencies. It pays monthly interest drawn from homeowner mortgage payments, with steadier quality than corporate debt but returns that shift as refinancing waves come and go.
DDV: Mostly Treasury securities and cash-like holdings, with a smaller slice of broad stock funds covering value, international and small companies. The mix targets a short, defined interest-rate profile, suiting cautious money that still wants a little growth.
CBTO: A structured outcome fund on bitcoin for a one-year period ending each October, taking part in bitcoin's gains up to a cap while adding protection against steep declines. It suits bitcoin-curious investors who want a defined payoff instead of the coin's full swings.
CBXJ: A structured outcome fund on bitcoin built from short-term Treasury securities and over-the-counter options, over a one-year period ending each January. It aims to join bitcoin's gains up to a cap while cushioning deep falls, so it moves far less than bitcoin itself.
ULTI: Options income strategies spread across a basket of mostly technology and other fast-moving US stocks, aiming to maximize regular payouts. The high income comes with capped gains on each position, and the speculative names underneath make it livelier than most income funds.
CDEI: Large US companies that score well on diversity, equity and inclusion under Calvert's responsible investment principles, spanning technology, finance and health care. It offers a core stock holding screened for workplace and governance practices, not just size and price.
XTAP: Options on the S&P 500 that aim to deliver accelerated gains up to a preset cap over a one-year period starting each April. It is a leveraged-style bet on a rising market, carrying full losses when the index falls.
MUNX: Intermediate-term municipal bonds from across the US, paying interest exempt from federal income tax, managed by a specialist muni team. It targets steady tax-free income with moderate price movement, sitting between short-term safety and long-term yield in the muni market.
RINF: A position built to gain when the market's expected inflation rate rises, using the gap between regular Treasury yields and inflation-protected Treasury yields. It is a targeted hedge against inflation surprises, and it loses ground when inflation expectations cool.
MILK: Corporate bonds issued by companies in Pacer's Cash Cows stock indexes, firms picked for generating strong free cash flow. The idea is that cash-rich companies are dependable borrowers, so their bonds pay interest with less worry about repayment.
GLDW: Leveraged exposure to gold through swap agreements and shares, aiming to amplify a gold fund's return each week while paying weekly distributions. The weekly reset and leverage make it a trading tool, and the distributions are not the same thing as profit.
OWNB: Companies that hold large amounts of bitcoin on their own balance sheets, the so-called bitcoin standard firms, including miners and software companies turned bitcoin treasuries. It rises and falls with bitcoin's price, with extra company-specific risk on top.
TFNS: Financial companies of every kind: banks, card networks, insurers, exchanges and investment firms. It is a focused bet on the finance industry, which tends to thrive when lending is healthy and suffer when credit problems spread.
MPLY: Companies with monopoly-like positions, dominant firms facing little competition in their markets, led by big technology platforms. It looks for pricing power and durability, and its concentration in a few dozen winners makes it more focused than a broad index fund.
TEXN: Companies headquartered in Texas, where energy is the biggest slice at about a third, with technology, industry and consumer firms behind. It is a single-state bet, so Texas's oil-driven economy and business climate drive the results.
FORH: Small and mid-sized companies worldwide, picked opportunistically across industry, technology, health care and energy, with some Treasury bills and volatility hedges alongside. The flexible, concentrated style means results depend heavily on the managers' calls.
CSRA: Real assets for income and inflation resistance: property companies, commodities, pipelines, utilities and gold, gathered through other funds and direct holdings. It aims to behave differently from plain stocks and bonds, especially when inflation is rising.
WDRN: Companies building physical artificial intelligence: humanoid robots, drones, self-driving systems and the chips and parts inside them. It is an early-stage theme where many holdings are small and unprofitable, so expect sharp swings.
SEA: Global cargo companies: container lines, oil tankers, ship owners, air freight and port operators. It is a bet on world trade volumes and shipping rates, which are famously cyclical, booming when ships are scarce and slumping when fleets grow.
RCLY: Middle slices of collateralized loan obligations, bundles of company loans, rated in the BBB to B range where yields are higher and risk is real. It pays stronger income than top-rated CLO funds, and it can fall hard if loan defaults climb.
DDTF: Options on the S&P 500 designed to gain from modest moves in either direction over a one-year period starting each February, with a 10 percent buffer against drops. It is built for choppy, sideways markets, and big one-way moves can leave it behind.
TLTI: Treasury bonds with more than 20 years to maturity, plus income from selling put options on the S&P 500. Long Treasuries already swing a lot when rates move, and the stock options add extra income along with extra risk in a stock sell-off.
RAAY: Leveraged exposure to the safest AAA slices of collateralized loan obligations, bundles of company loans, with leverage used to enhance the yield. The top-rated collateral keeps credit risk low, but the borrowed money magnifies price moves in both directions.
RAAR: Leveraged exposure to AAA collateralized loan obligation slices, the safest layer of bundles of company loans, with distributions reinvested rather than paid out. Reinvesting compounds the yield over time, while the leverage still magnifies every price move.
TLDR: A ladder of Treasury bills, the shortest-term US government debt, with maturities spread out over six months or less. It is a cash-like parking spot that pays a bit of interest, with safety and daily access as the point.
DDTJ: Options on the S&P 500 designed to gain from modest moves in either direction over a one-year period starting each January, with a 10 percent buffer against drops. It is built for choppy, sideways markets, and big one-way moves can leave it behind.
KROP: Companies modernizing farming and food: tractor and machinery makers, seed and crop science, fertilizers and food innovators around the world. It is a bet on feeding more people with fewer resources, tied to farm incomes and crop prices.
SEF: A daily inverse bet on financial stocks, designed to rise when bank and finance shares in the S&P 500 fall. It resets daily, so it is a short-term hedge or trade, and it steadily loses ground when financial stocks climb.
RJVI: Income gathered from every layer of a company's finances, its bonds, preferred shares and common stock, mostly investment grade corporate debt. This vertical approach lets the managers pick whichever layer of a trusted company pays best at the time.
FFLV: Large US companies trading at value prices, chosen with Fidelity's fundamental research across technology, finance, health care and consumer shares. It includes some big technology names bought when they looked cheap, so it is less strictly old-economy than many value funds.
ZTWO: Investment grade corporate bonds with roughly two years left until they mature. The short lifespan keeps price swings small when interest rates move, making it a steadier income holding than longer corporate bond funds.
MPDY: Exposure through swap contracts to an autocall index tied to S&P 500 futures with a built-in volatility target. It aims to pay regular coupon income and can be called away early, with returns depending on the stock market staying above set levels.
SCAP: Small US companies chosen for income, including dividend-paying stocks and a large slice of preferred shares across industry, technology, retail and finance. Income from small caps is uncommon, and the preferred holdings add both yield and interest-rate sensitivity.
CHYG: High yield corporate bonds with five years or less to maturity, the shorter end of the junk bond market. Shorter maturities mean less damage when interest rates rise, though the below-investment-grade credit risk remains fully in place.
MIG: Investment grade corporate bonds chosen with Moody's Analytics credit research, which looks for bonds priced attractively for their risk. It aims for a steadier, better-screened core corporate bond holding than a plain index of the whole market.
